analysis.one_liner: Requires paid 15-minute rest breaks for construction workers every four hours.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote: it sat in the Education and the Workforce Committee until the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to require employers to give construction employees at least one paid 15-minute break for every four hours worked. It would also require employers to tell new hires about the right in their primary language, post bilingual signs at work sites, and ban firing or punishing workers who take breaks or file complaints with the Labor Department. Employers who violate the rules would face Labor Department penalties and, for retaliation, back pay plus an equal amount in damages. It was introduced in February 2023 and referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction workers, including contractors hired for general construction work, who would get a guaranteed paid break every four hours, notice of the right in their own language, and protection from retaliation if they complain.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must provide at least one 15-minute paid rest break for every four hours of work to each construction employee [S2][S3].
At hiring, employers must explain the break right in the employee's primary language and post signs about it in English and Spanish at work sites [S2][S3].

Employers may not retaliate against or discriminate against workers who request breaks or file complaints with the Department of Labor, and violators owe back pay plus an equal amount in liquidated damages [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction employers, who would pay workers for about 15 extra paid minutes per four-hour shift, post notices, and face federal penalties if they fail to comply or punish workers for taking breaks.

drawbacks.text: The break requirement would raise labor costs for construction firms, a cost that could be passed on to customers through higher bids or absorbed through reduced scheduling flexibility [S3].

The bill sets a low floor — one break per four hours — which would do nothing in states with stronger break laws and only preempts weaker rules, since it explicitly does not excuse compliance with any law or contract requiring longer breaks [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is concrete and modest: a guaranteed paid break during physically demanding work, with real teeth against retaliation. The cost to employers is limited to roughly 15 minutes of paid time per four hours of work plus posting requirements. The bill is narrow — it covers only construction workers and does not touch other industries — but within its scope the benefits outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up or sent it to the floor before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sylvia Garcia introduced the bill on February 2, 2023 with 12 original cosponsors, all House Democrats [S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction employers are better off because the bill died: they avoid paying for 15 minutes of break time per four hours of work and the new penalties. Construction workers gained nothing.

for.name: Sylvia R. Garcia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought 12 Democratic colleagues on as original cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never held a markup or advanced the bill to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 13 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record, and the House committee where the bill stalled had a Republican majority in this Congress [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would make them pay for about 15 minutes of break time per four-hour shift and face Labor Department penalties for violations or retaliation. Their gain from the bill dying is the cost workers would have received in guaranteed paid rest.
